content.text: Explore the reflex arc — trace the pathway from stimulus to response through receptor, relay, and effector neurones using the interactive visualisation below.
By the end of this lesson, you should be able to:
Define a reflex and explain why reflexes are important
Describe the components of a reflex arc
Explain the pathway of a simple reflex
Give examples of different types of reflexes

is an automatic, rapid response to a stimulus that does not involve conscious thought. Reflexes are protective and allow the body to respond quickly to potentially dangerous situations. The neural pathway that enables a reflex is called a

Involves the spinal cord (or brain stem)

content.text: The Pathway of a Simple Reflex
Receptor: Thermoreceptor in skin detects heat
Sensory neurone: Carries impulse to spinal cord
Relay neurone: Passes impulse (in spinal cord)
Motor neurone: Carries impulse to muscle
Response: Hand pulls away from hot object
Brain can be informed (but response doesn't wait)
Tests the nervous system is working
Exaggerated = possible upper motor neurone problem
Reflex happens BEFORE you're consciously aware
Relay neurones also send impulses to brain
You feel pain AFTER you've already moved
This is why reflexes are so fast
Sensory neurones to brain (via optic nerve)
You can keep your hand on something hot deliberately
You can stop yourself from blinking
Brain can inhibit the reflex arc
Most spinal reflexes bypass the brain for the response (brain is informed after)
Reflexes are specific involuntary responses; habits are different
Some reflexes like the knee-jerk cannot be voluntarily suppressed
Reflexes are slow because they involve multiple neurones
Reflexes are very fast; the synaptic delay is minimal
Automatic, rapid response to a stimulus
Pathway of neurones involved in a reflex
Carries impulses from receptor to CNS
Connects sensory and motor neurones in CNS
Carries impulses from CNS to effector
Muscle or gland that produces a response
Change in pupil size in response to light
Reflexes are rapid, automatic, involuntary responses
They protect the body from harm
Reflex arc: receptor → sensory neurone → relay neurone → motor neurone → effector
Most reflexes are coordinated by spinal cord (not brain)
You become aware of the stimulus AFTER the reflex response
Examples: withdrawal reflex, pupil reflex, knee-jerk, blinking
Some reflexes can be voluntarily suppressed; others cannot
